overview: This atlas record is best read as a window onto Japan during the late Muromachi period, after the Onin War and amid the early Sengoku age. It was not a unified empire: Ashikaga shoguns remained important in Kyoto, but regional daimyo, military brokers, religious institutions, towns, villages and the imperial court all exercised power. Trade, craft, farming, scholarship and art continued through recurrent conflict. The 1492 start and 1530 end are map-library choices, not the birth or collapse of Japan; the Ashikaga shogunate itself lasted until 1573.

periods.title: After the Onin War, before the Meio coup
periods.summary: The atlas begins inside the late Muromachi period. Kyoto had been devastated, Ashikaga authority was weak, and powerful regional daimyo already shaped politics; 1492 is not the founding of Japan or the start of Sengoku conflict.

periods.title: The Meio coup and competing Ashikaga-Hosokawa power
periods.summary: In 1493 Yoshitane was deposed after marching to Kawachi, and Hosokawa Masamoto became the dominant broker around the shogunate. The coup changed who controlled the office; it did not create one government able to command every province.

periods.title: Restoration and renewed factional war around Kyoto
periods.summary: Shogunal and Hosokawa factions kept fighting. Kyoto City records the 1511 Battle of Funaokayama at a northern entrance to the capital, a reminder that the city remained a political prize and a lived-in place exposed to war.

periods.title: Yoshiharu, trade rivalry and a pictured capital
periods.summary: The twelfth shogun Yoshiharu occupied a 1525 Kyoto residence shown on the surviving city screen. Meanwhile Hosokawa and Ouchi competition over licensed Ming missions helped produce the violent Ningbo incident of 1523.

periods.title: A shogun outside Kyoto and a rival centre at Sakai
periods.summary: A rival Ashikaga-Hosokawa-Miyoshi power formed at Sakai in 1527 while Yoshiharu’s side operated away from Kyoto. Historians debate whether “Sakai bakufu” is the right label, so this card describes competing centres rather than declaring a settled replacement government.

sections.title: What this map shape means, and what it does not

items.text: The indexed record is exactly japan, circa 1492 to 1530, with two observed map intervals. Its generated aliases “Empire of Japan” and “Japanese Empire” belong to a much later age and are not used here. The content audit marks this exact record as missing before integration.

Both target maps are broad four-part MultiPolygons covering Kyushu, Shikoku, Honshu and Hokkaido. The 1492 version has 324 positions; the 1500 version has 329. These coast-scale shapes do not draw daimyo domains, temple lands, estates, town jurisdictions or front lines.

Hokkaido is the clearest atlas glitch. In 1400 it lies in the separate Ainu feature; in 1492 and 1500 the same broad island is moved into japan; in 1530 it returns to ainu-1530. Museum history instead shows Ainu societies, trade, Wajin settlements in the south and conflict, not Ashikaga control of the whole island.

Okinawa and Shuri fall outside every target polygon. That matches an essential political distinction: the independent Ryukyu Kingdom, unified in 1429 and ruled by the Second Sho dynasty from 1469, was pursuing its own diplomacy, trade and building under King Sho Shin. It must not be folded into this card’s “Japan.”

Kyoto, Sakai, Ashikaga School and the future Iwami mine all test inside the imported outline, but point-in-polygon only answers where the atlas drew them. It does not prove that the shogun governed each place in the same way. Political authority was negotiated among court, shogun, daimyo, temples, towns and local communities.

The 1467-1477 Onin War ended before this card but shaped everything that followed. Kyoto had been devastated and Ashikaga power badly weakened. Provincial daimyo retained substantial power, so a single colored outline should be read as a chronological label, not proof of a unified chain of command.

In 1493, shogun Yoshitane left Kyoto to intervene in a succession conflict in Kawachi. A coup led by Hosokawa Masamoto deposed him. The event shows how the shogun’s title mattered while military brokers could decide who held it; “Japan” was not a modern centralized nation-state.

Kyoto City records fighting at Funaokayama in 1511, near an approach from Tamba. Battles around the capital affected more than famous warriors: fires, disrupted roads and armed compounds touched the same urban landscape where households, markets, workshops and religious institutions continued to function.

Farmers and other villagers were political actors too. The National Museum’s medieval gallery explains that communities made demands and sometimes fought warriors, while regional daimyo tried to consolidate rule. “Warring States” therefore involved negotiation, collective action and local organization as well as battles between lords.

From 1527, an Ashikaga claimant, Hosokawa Harumoto and Miyoshi Motonaga operated from Sakai while Yoshiharu’s camp was displaced. One historian calls this a “Sakai bakufu,” but the NDL reference page labels that name a hypothesis. The safest picture is overlapping rival centres, not a clean nationwide transfer.

sections.title: Ports, money, mines and long-distance exchange

items.text: Licensed trade with Ming China worked through tallies and tributary diplomacy. The shogunate used the title “king of Japan” to fit Ming rules, while actual ship management involved daimyo, temples, shrines and merchants. Diplomatic language, commercial profit and decentralized power travelled on the same ships.

A wind-driven crossing to China took at least a month, and waiting for winds plus overland travel could stretch a round trip across years. Japan exported sulfur, swords and fans and imported silk and copper coins. There was no standard Japanese-minted currency, so money itself was an import.

The Hosokawa and Ouchi competed over rights to Ming missions, and their rivalry led to the Ningbo incident in 1523. Modern scholarship cautions against turning the aftermath into a simple story of one family’s monopoly. Foreign trade was valuable, political and sometimes violent.

Sakai grew as a trading and self-governing city; merchant councillors appear in records by 1484. Archaeology also records repeated disaster: large fires in 1494, 1508 and 1526. A prosperous port could be connected, wealthy and politically assertive while rebuilding over and over.

Iwami Ginzan’s documented discovery and early development begin in 1526, near this card’s end. Ore first went by land to Tomogaura and then by sea to Hakata. The famous cupellation technique arrived in 1533, so the mine’s huge later production must not be pulled backward into 1492-1530.

sections.title: Work, food, houses and what people wore

items.text: The National Museum’s child-focused gallery shows women from Katsura selling ayu fish in Kyoto, large saws derived from China making lengthwise timber cutting easier, and water wheels lifting water into paddies. These examples make “technology” concrete: baskets, blades and water power changed ordinary work.

At Ichijodani, excavators found sea-bream bones with knife marks, shells, seeds and charred rice. Knives, iron pots and grinding bowls survived too. This one castle town joined fields, forests and the Japan Sea in its diet; it is evidence for a place, not a menu eaten by everyone.

A chopping board at Ichijodani had once been a serving tray, and inexpensive lacquer bowls were mass produced for everyday meals. Medieval recycling could be extremely practical: when a tray retired from table duty, it apparently applied for a second career under the kitchen knife.

Sakai excavations reveal narrow, deep homes for ordinary merchants and craftspeople, along with pots, pans, chopsticks, buckets and both local and imported ceramics. Some wealthy merchants had large compounds and storehouses. Urban housing therefore ranged widely, and the excavated layers extend beyond this exact card.

The 1525 Kyoto-screen database catalogues 1,426 painted figures by age group, occupation, clothing, headgear, hairstyle, object and activity. It records kosode, hats, veils, tied and shaved hair among many choices. The classifications help us inspect social difference, but a painted crowd is not a population survey.

sections.title: Families, women, children and time together

items.text: Family authority did not follow one simple rule. A museum study finds men increasingly represented households in later fifteenth-century property documents, yet sixteenth-century pictures often show widow nuns leading women or whole families. Class, region, life stage and the survival of records all shape what historians can see.

The 1525 screen shows an aristocratic residence with a woman interpreted as the householder’s wife and a girl wearing her hair in two buns. They watch a bird-song contest beside flowering plum. This is a lovely glimpse of elite family sociability, with the museum’s “probably” labels kept intact.

Elsewhere on the same screen, women in kazuki veils walk along Shinmachi Street while children lead dogs. That does not prove every child had a pet. It does prove the artist considered children, dogs and street life worth painting, which may be history’s oldest surviving Kyoto dog-walk cameo.

Elite warrior boys often went through genpuku between about eleven and seventeen, receiving an adult name and hearing stories of martial achievement. Some lower-ranking warriors marked adulthood by shaving the front and crown of the head. Medieval graduation could involve more haircut and renaming than homework.

A painted Kanze Noh stage has men and women standing around its open sides as two actors cross the bridgeway. Kyoto townspeople also revived the Gion festival in 1500 after wartime interruption. Performance and festival offered shared time, though access and experience differed by wealth and status.

sections.title: Learning, art and a real line of writing

items.text: Ashikaga School students studied Confucian learning, divination and later military strategy. There was no modern timetable: students copied classical Chinese books and largely studied on their own. Rules required clerical status. This specialized institution is evidence of advanced learning, not proof that most children attended school.

The renga poet Socho visited Ashikaga School in 1509. Its lecture and study halls then burned sometime between 1528 and 1531, a date range that crosses this card’s endpoint. Books and institutions could connect distant scholars, yet fire and war made learning spaces physically fragile.

Written-language sample: くはうさま. Letter by letter this is ku-hau-sama; the museum glosses it 公方様, conventionally read kubō-sama, “the lord” or here “the shogun.” It is hiragana on the 1525 Kyoto screen, using historical spelling and usually unmarked voicing. Hiragana is a Japanese syllabary developed from cursive forms of Chinese characters.

Sesshu’s 1495 Splashed-Ink Landscape suggests mountains with a few rough brushstrokes. Around 1513, Kano Motonobu adapted Chinese-derived ink conventions with Japanese decorative methods. These famous surviving works show artistic experimentation and patronage; they tell us much less about what hung in an ordinary home.

The 1525 Kyoto screen turns an entire city into its subject, including commoners and elites in daily movement. Its 1,426 catalogued figures are an extraordinary achievement of observation and later research. The artist still selected, arranged and stylized the view, so absence from the screen is not absence from history.

A 1468 work called Enju Ruiyo treated nutrition and health care, showing that learned medicine joined food and the body in written study. The listed surviving object is a 1793 transcription. One copied medical book cannot tell us who obtained treatment, how practitioners worked locally or whether a remedy helped.

Later medical historians read a Kyoto physician’s text as describing a syphilis outbreak in 1512 and a Kanto temple record as describing another in 1513. This is serious evidence of a new epidemic, but the diagnosis, transmission route and “first arrival” date are retrospective scholarly interpretations rather than modern laboratory results.

Tea sat between medicine, sociability and display. It still carried a medicinal reputation, but people also played tea-origin guessing games, and sixteenth-century samurai and merchants ordered specialist kettles for ceremonies. A warm drink could be treatment, competition and hospitality, depending on the cup and company.

Sakai archaeology finds packed-earth roads with rain drains, tile- or pottery-lined wells and unglazed jars buried as latrine tanks beside streets, probably so waste could be collected for fertilizer. This is excellent toilet evidence for one city across layered dates. It does not establish islandwide sewers, equal clean-water access or modern sanitation.

Water systems were local labor, not invisible magic. Rural water-lifting wheels moved irrigation water from lower ground into paddies. Surviving evidence is uneven, so the honest answer for many villages and households is simply that their detailed water and waste arrangements are not yet known.

sections.title: Objects, neighbours and what continued after 1530

items.text: A wheel-thrown Seto- or Mino-ware tea bowl dated 1510-1530 combined features admired in different Chinese ceramics. It is a small technological and artistic achievement: potters transformed imported models into locally made wares. Its glittering lacquer repairs are later, so they are not evidence for this card’s own years.

Muromachi achievements were not only military. Commercial and transport networks expanded while patrons supported linked verse, Noh, tea, gardens and ink painting. Many celebrated objects come from elites or temples, however, so “cultural flourishing” should not erase hunger, forced service, fire, epidemic or the destruction caused by war.

The 1525 screen is crowded with seasons, ceremonies, trades, homes and streets. It is tempting to call it a photograph, but it is better treated as a brilliantly organized argument about a city. Historians can compare its details with documents and excavation without assuming every painted gesture happened at one moment.

Ainu people did not enter history only when an atlas moved a polygon, and they did not disappear when it moved back. The National Ainu Museum presents Ainu language, life, history, work and exchange from Ainu perspectives into the present. The Hokkaido geometry problem is therefore both cartographic and human.

In 1530 the atlas relabels the three main islands japan-warring-states and returns Hokkaido to an Ainu feature. No state ended that year. Conflict was already under way, the Ashikaga shogunate continued until 1573, and the existing later card takes over from this artificial cutoff. People, towns, farms, arts and institutions continued.

ending.text: The map changes labels in 1530, but neither Japan nor the Ashikaga political world ended then. The successor polygon is nearly the same across Kyushu, Shikoku and Honshu, while Hokkaido is reassigned to an Ainu feature. Conflict continued, and the Ashikaga shogunate remained until 1573. This card hands the atlas chronology to japan-warring-states without pretending that one country vanished or a new people appeared at midnight on 1 January 1530.
